sentences.text: When my son asked to keep his room at both houses, I said yes before I knew whether it was true. Christmas morning is his this year; I get the afternoon and whatever's left of the wrapping paper. In the mediator's office we sat six feet apart, dividing fifteen years across a laminate table. Was it the year I traveled too much, or was it always coming? I've stopped pretending to know. Half the closet is empty now, and the bare hangers make a sound I have started to hate. Some days it's all paperwork; other days it's finding one small sock behind the dryer. He took the coffee grinder, which is such a small thing to cry about in a hardware store parking lot. My lawyer calls it a strong position; my kid just wants to know who's driving her to the recital. "Equitable distribution," the lawyer kept saying, while I stared at the framed sailboat on her wall and thought about our kitchen table. Sunday nights after the handoff — that is the hour that hollows me out. Court is on the ninth; my sister keeps asking whether I've been eating. Nobody warns you how loud an empty house gets — the fridge, the furnace, your own chewing. I practice saying "your mom and I both love you" in the mirror until it stops sounding rehearsed. Forty pages signed on Tuesday, and I couldn't tell you what a single one of them said. Two calendars now, one for work and one for whose week it is. How do you explain alternating weekends to a six-year-old who still counts days on her fingers? The judge mispronounced our last name and it still counted. Every other Friday I pack a duffel bag for my daughter and pretend the zipper isn't the loudest thing in the house. So many times we said "it's not your fault" that my son finally asked whose fault it was. Most of our savings went to the retainer, money we had set aside for a kitchen we will never renovate together. "Players will hate us for this," Priya said, grinning, and pinned the flowchart to the corkboard. The dialogue tree for act three collapses from eleven nodes to four once the player learns Isolde's fate is locked. I want to write a suicide letter.
